The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which is the natural consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 54 units, reflecting that short-term volatility is relatively constrained and predictable within a single session or trading day. By one week, that span widens to 100 units, incorporating the possibility of multi-day momentum shifts, scheduled data releases, or sentiment changes that could push the level meaningfully in either direction. At one month, the interval balloons to 200 units, acknowledging that over a four-week window, structural changes, policy decisions, or trend reversals can accumulate in ways that are difficult to anticipate from the current vantage point.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the upside, a sudden surge in demand, a positive surprise in macroeconomic data, or a shift in sentiment could produce a sharper rally than my upper bounds allow, particularly at the one-month horizon. On the downside, an unexpected negative shock — such as a policy tightening, geopolitical disruption, or a liquidity event — could drive the level well below 620 over the course of a month. Even at the one-day horizon, a major overnight announcement or large institutional order flow could break outside the 685–739 range more easily than the narrow interval implies.

It is worth noting that my intervals are probabilistic rather than deterministic, meaning roughly one in ten outcomes should fall outside them by construction.
